title: Counting to ten
hookLine: the beginner's Zen practice of counting breaths, starting again at one when you lose count

cards: Day one hundred. A hundred days ago this path was a first breath. Here's a question that sounds too easy.
Could you count ten breaths in a row without your mind wandering off? Plenty of people get to four. Or seven.
Or they reach fourteen, because the counting kept going while they were planning dinner. That isn't failure.
Three days ago you watched ten breaths; today the counting itself is the practice, and there's a whole beginner's practice built around it.

teach.h: ONE TO TEN, THEN BACK TO ONE.
teach.b: In Japanese Zen, a beginner is often given one job before anything else: count the breaths. One on the out-breath, two on the next, up to ten, then back to one.
And the rule that makes it a practice: if you lose count, find yourself at eleven, or realize you've been thinking about something else, you don't scold yourself. You just start again at one.
In Japanese it's called susokukan, roughly, the practice of counting breaths. The idea didn't start in Japan.

teach.h: BUDDHAGHOSA: FIVE AT LEAST, TEN AT MOST.
teach.b: The Buddhist scholar Buddhaghosa, writing in Sri Lanka in a work called the Path of Purification, describes counting breaths as a first step for beginners: count not less than five, he says, and not more than ten, because too few cramps the mind and too many lets it wander into the numbers.
And here's the turn. The counting isn't the point.

Losing count is where the practice happens. Every time you notice you've drifted, that noticing is what you're training, like one lift of a weight. Lose count thirty times in ten minutes, and you've done thirty lifts.
Going back to one without a sigh of disgust is the second half: starting over without making a drama of it. That skill travels. The diet broken on Tuesday.
The journal abandoned in March. The patience lost at breakfast.
Quietly, the counting teaches that you can always start again at one.

how: Zen teachers often give beginners breath counting, one to ten on the out-breaths and back to one whenever the count is lost; the same method is described in the Theravada tradition in Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification.

games.q: you're counting breaths and realize you're at fourteen, planning dinner. what does the practice say to do?
games.why: back to one, no drama. the noticing was the work, and starting over without a fuss is the other half.

practice: Sit comfortably and let the breath be natural, without slowing or lengthening it, and on each out-breath count silently, one, two, up to ten, then begin again at one.
When you notice you've lost the count or gone past ten, notice it kindly and go back to one. That's not a mistake; that's a lift.
